findings.title: Raw recovery codes are sent to user storage while local storage keeps hashed codes
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes `generatedCodes` (the plaintext codes shown to the user) and passes that JSON to `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`. The local-DB path instead goes through `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel)`, where the codes are hashed (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode exists for this). So the same credential is stored as plaintext in external user storage but as hashed in the Keycloak DB. Plaintext recovery codes are secrets, and this exposes them to the external store and any reader of it. The user-storage path should store the same hashed representation, or the design should be explicitly documented and justified.

findings.title: Recovery codes validated in user storage are never consumed, so they can be reused
findings.body: isValid for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE only checks that the code is present in the stored list and never marks it as used or removes it. The authenticator (RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator) relies on the credential's used-code state to decide when to remove the credential and re-trigger code generation, and that state is never updated for user-storage credentials. Each recovery code can therefore be used indefinitely against this provider, and allCodesUsed() is never true for it. The reference provider should consume codes the same way the local provider does, or the limitation should be documented.

findings.title: getCredential fallback ignores where a removed federated credential would be deleted
findings.body: The authenticator later calls credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(id) on the credential returned by getCredential. If that credential came from the federated (user storage) stream, the removal targets local storage, where the ID does not exist, so the exhausted codes credential is never removed from user storage. The removal path should check which store the credential came from.

findings.title: getCredentials dereferences myUser without a null check
findings.body: getMyUser(user) can return null when the user is not in the in-memory map, and getCredentials then calls myUser.recoveryCodes and myUser.otp, causing a NullPointerException. Other methods in this class (for example getDisableableCredentialTypesStream and isConfiguredFor) guard against a null MyUser.

findings.title: Recovery-keys test only covers the happy path
findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin sets up codes and logs in once with a valid code. It does not check that an invalid code is rejected, that a used code cannot be reused, or that the required action is re-triggered when all codes are used. Those are the behaviours the user-storage change is meant to get right, and the reuse case is exactly where the provider currently fails.
